title: Stuck then recovers
description: A maths student gets stuck, receives hints, and eventually solves the proof.

event.text: I'm not sure where to start with this. How do I prove that root two is irrational?

mock.evidence: Student says they don't know how to start.

event.text: OK, so I'll assume that root two equals p over q, where p and q are integers with no common factors - they're in lowest terms.

mock.evidence: Correctly assumes p/q in lowest terms.

event.text: If I square both sides, I get p squared equals two q squared. That means p squared is even, so p must be even because an odd number squared is odd.

mock.evidence: Correctly deduces p is even from p² = 2q².

event.text: So if p is even, I can write p equals two k for some integer k. Then substituting gives four k squared equals two q squared, so two k squared equals q squared. That means q is even too. But that's a contradiction because I assumed they had no common factors!
For the square root of four, let me think - if root four equals p over q, then p squared equals four q squared. That doesn't give us a contradiction like before, because four is a perfect square.

mock.evidence: Correctly identifies why the proof doesn't work for √4.
